<div class="big-question">Which distinctions between histories change the distribution over futures?</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: under 1 minute.
- This slide is primarily for the instructor's pacing decision.
- The final block may be 45 or 60 minutes; do not turn all available time into slide lecture.
:::

## Four lenses on predictive state

<div class="grid-4">
<div class="card blue"><h3>HMM belief</h3><p>Posterior over a chosen model's hidden states.</p><p><strong>Update:</strong> normalize a stochastic propagation.</p></div>
<div class="card green"><h3>Conditional Hankel row</h3><p>Probabilities of all future tests.</p><p><strong>Update:</strong> condition after appending a symbol.</p></div>
<div class="card purple"><h3>Finite PSR</h3><p>Probabilities of selected spanning tests.</p><p><strong>Update:</strong> generally rational after normalization.</p></div>
<div class="card orange"><h3>WFA state</h3><p>Coordinates in a finite linear basis.</p><p><strong>Update:</strong> linear symbol operators.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">Different coordinates can describe the same observable predictive distinctions.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: about 2 minutes.
- Ask one student to name what each coordinate refers to.
- Avoid ranking these as increasingly “real”; they serve different calculational and interpretive roles.
:::

## What survives a change of coordinates?

<div class="big-question">Every valid realization assigns the same probability to every finite word.</div>

<div class="equation-panel">
$$
\Pr(w)\quad\text{is invariant; coordinates, update matrices, and arbitrary metric geometry need not be.}
$$
</div>

<div class="grid-3">
<div class="card green"><h3>Invariant</h3><p>word probabilities and full predictive equivalence</p></div>
<div class="card gold"><h3>Representation-dependent</h3><p>state labels, redundant directions, and basis entries</p></div>
<div class="card orange"><h3>Requires care</h3><p>Euclidean geometry after an arbitrary invertible transform</p></div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: about 2 minutes.
- Connect this to affine transformer probes: an affine relation is meaningful evidence, but raw axes are not canonical.
- Predictive equivalence is process-relative; HMM belief equality can be finer than needed.
:::

## What the transformer evidence supports

<div class="evidence-ladder">
  <div class="rung"><span class="number">1</span><span>Belief coordinates are <strong>affinely decodable</strong> from activations in the studied toy processes.</span><span class="status">supported</span></div>
  <div class="rung"><span class="number">2</span><span>Structure changes with training and survives held-out and shuffle comparisons.</span><span class="status">supported</span></div>
  <div class="rung"><span class="number">3</span><span>RRXOR geometry distinguishes histories beyond current optimal next-token distributions.</span><span class="status">supported</span></div>
  <div class="rung"><span class="number">4</span><span>The decoded directions are used causally to implement Bayesian updating.</span><span class="status">not directly tested</span></div>
</div>

<div class="source-line">Shai et al., NeurIPS 2024, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15943">arXiv:2405.15943</a>.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: about 2 minutes.
- Keep “studied toy processes” audible; do not generalize to transformers broadly.
- The last rung is an experiment design opportunity, not a defect to hand-wave away.
:::

## Five caveats worth retaining

<div class="grid-2">
<div class="card gold"><h3>1 · Belief is model-relative</h3><p>An HMM posterior depends on the chosen realization.</p></div>
<div class="card gold"><h3>2 · One step is not every future</h3><p>Matched next-token predictions can hide longer-future differences.</p></div>
<div class="card gold"><h3>3 · A finite block is local evidence</h3><p>Its dependencies need not determine full Hankel rank.</p></div>
<div class="card gold"><h3>4 · Linear dimension is not HMM size</h3><p>A finite linear realization need not be nonnegative and stochastic.</p></div>
</div>

<div class="card orange" style="margin-top:0.55em;"><h3>5 · Decodability is not causal use</h3><p>A diagnostic map can reveal information without proving the model's forward computation relies on that coordinate.</p></div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: about 2 minutes.
- These are the five places students are most likely to overstate the day’s conclusions.
- If time is short, ask students to choose the caveat they think matters most and defend it.
:::

## Optional branch: append a symbol linearly

<div class="gate">
<span class="label">Open only if time remains</span>
<p>Return to the Notebook 3 instructor demo. Give students the observable basis blocks and solved symbol operators; do not assign matrix inversion.</p>
</div>

<div class="grid-2">
<div class="card purple">
<h3>Basis row</h3>
<p>A finite vector records selected observable tests after a history.</p>
</div>
<div class="card blue">
<h3>Symbol operator</h3>
<p>Multiplying by $A_x$ updates that linear coordinate when symbol $x$ is appended.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="equation-panel">
$$
\Pr(x_1\cdots x_L)=\alpha A_{x_1}\cdots A_{x_L}\omega.
$$
</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: at most 1 minute of setup here, then 5–6 minutes for the supplied notebook word check.
- Students should verify one supplied word and interpret the representation; do not assign reconstruction or matrix inversion.
- This branch depends on the core factorization; omit it if that dependency is missing.
:::

## Negative entries are not negative probabilities

<div class="grid-2">
<div class="card orange">
<h3>What an operator entry is</h3>
<p>A coefficient in an observable linear coordinate update.</p>
</div>
<div class="card green">
<h3>What the induced word weights must satisfy</h3>
<p>Nonnegativity, normalization at every length, and extension consistency:</p>
<p>$P(w)\geq 0$, $\sum_{|w|=L}P(w)=1$, and $P(u)=\sum_x P(ux)$.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="takeaway">A weighted finite automaton is a linear realization of the process—not automatically a hidden Markov model.</div>

::: {.notes}
- Target: under 1 minute after the notebook word check.
- Ask students why an intermediate negative coordinate is harmless if the complete observable evaluation stays valid.
- Do not describe the operators as transition probabilities.
:::

## Three questions worth carrying forward

<div class="question-list">
  <div class="question">Which predictive coordinates are actually used causally inside a trained model?</div>
  <div class="question">Which parts of representation geometry survive principled changes of basis?</div>
  <div class="question">When does finite predictive dimension admit a compact nonnegative realization?</div>
</div>

<div class="handoff">
<span class="label">Closing invariant</span>
<p>Whatever coordinates we choose, the observable process is the set of probabilities assigned to finite words.</p>
</div>
